meaning: Individuals of the same species occupying a defined area during a defined time.
example: The breeding rabbits in a specified valley during one season form the study population.
importantDistinction: A population boundary must be stated before counting frequencies.
whatItDoes: The breeding rabbits in a specified valley during one season form the study population.
feature: The breeding rabbits in a specified valley during one season form the study population.
confusion: A population boundary must be stated before counting frequencies.

meaning: All the alleles present in the reproductive population being considered.
example: A population contains several alleles at many different loci.
importantDistinction: A gene pool describes a population, not only one individual’s genotype.
whatItDoes: A population contains several alleles at many different loci.
feature: A population contains several alleles at many different loci.
confusion: A gene pool describes a population, not only one individual’s genotype.

meaning: Differences in genetic information among individuals or lineages.
example: Individuals carry different alleles at a pigment locus.
importantDistinction: Not all phenotypic variation is genetic.
whatItDoes: Individuals carry different alleles at a pigment locus.
feature: Individuals carry different alleles at a pigment locus.
confusion: Not all phenotypic variation is genetic.

meaning: A change in allele frequencies in a population across generations.
example: An allele’s proportion changes from 0.30 to 0.45 between sampled generations.
importantDistinction: A larger population can retain the same allele frequencies.
whatItDoes: An allele’s proportion changes from 0.30 to 0.45 between sampled generations.
feature: An allele’s proportion changes from 0.30 to 0.45 between sampled generations.
confusion: A larger population can retain the same allele frequencies.

meaning: The proportion of individuals with a specified genotype.
example: Thirty AA individuals in a population of 100 give frequency 0.30.
importantDistinction: Its denominator is the number of individuals sampled.
whatItDoes: Thirty AA individuals in a population of 100 give frequency 0.30.
feature: Thirty AA individuals in a population of 100 give frequency 0.30.
confusion: Its denominator is the number of individuals sampled.

meaning: The proportion of allele copies represented by a particular allele at a locus.
example: Twenty A copies among 50 copies give frequency 0.40.
importantDistinction: For an ordinary diploid autosomal sample, the denominator is 2N.
whatItDoes: Twenty A copies among 50 copies give frequency 0.40.
feature: Twenty A copies among 50 copies give frequency 0.40.
confusion: For an ordinary diploid autosomal sample, the denominator is 2N.

meaning: The contribution of one copy of each allele from a heterozygous individual.
example: Each Aa individual contributes one A and one a to the allele count.
importantDistinction: Count both copies, not half an individual.
whatItDoes: Each Aa individual contributes one A and one a to the allele count.
feature: Each Aa individual contributes one A and one a to the allele count.
confusion: Count both copies, not half an individual.

meaning: The requirement that mutually exclusive complete categories account for the whole sample.
example: At a two-allele locus, p + q = 1.
importantDistinction: The relevant categories and denominator must be consistent.
whatItDoes: At a two-allele locus, p + q = 1.
feature: At a two-allele locus, p + q = 1.
confusion: The relevant categories and denominator must be consistent.

meaning: A model in which allele frequencies remain constant and genotype frequencies follow p², 2pq and q² under stated conditions.
example: A large randomly mating population with no selection, migration or mutation is the reference model.
importantDistinction: The model is a baseline to test, not an automatic property of every population.
whatItDoes: A large randomly mating population with no selection, migration or mutation is the reference model.
feature: A large randomly mating population with no selection, migration or mutation is the reference model.
confusion: The model is a baseline to test, not an automatic property of every population.

meaning: Mating that is independent of the genotype being considered.
example: Gamete combinations can be modelled from allele frequencies without genotype-based mate preference.
importantDistinction: Random mating at one locus does not mean every behaviour is random.
whatItDoes: Gamete combinations can be modelled from allele frequencies without genotype-based mate preference.
feature: Gamete combinations can be modelled from allele frequencies without genotype-based mate preference.
confusion: Random mating at one locus does not mean every behaviour is random.

meaning: The expected frequency of one homozygous genotype under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
example: If p = 0.70, the expected AA frequency is 0.49.
importantDistinction: It is an expected genotype frequency, not another allele frequency.
whatItDoes: If p = 0.70, the expected AA frequency is 0.49.
feature: If p = 0.70, the expected AA frequency is 0.49.
confusion: It is an expected genotype frequency, not another allele frequency.

meaning: The expected heterozygote frequency under the two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
example: Aa can form from A then a or a then A.
importantDistinction: The factor two counts the two ways to form a heterozygote.
whatItDoes: Aa can form from A then a or a then A.
feature: Aa can form from A then a or a then A.
confusion: The factor two counts the two ways to form a heterozygote.

meaning: The expected aa genotype frequency under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
example: If q is 0.40, q² is 0.16.
importantDistinction: A recessive phenotype fraction can be used as q² only with the appropriate model.
whatItDoes: If q is 0.40, q² is 0.16.
feature: If q is 0.40, q² is 0.16.
confusion: A recessive phenotype fraction can be used as q² only with the appropriate model.

meaning: The proportion of heterozygotes carrying a recessive allele in the stated model.
example: For Hardy–Weinberg p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, carriers have frequency 0.48.
importantDistinction: For this simple recessive model, carriers are heterozygotes, not all individuals with a.
whatItDoes: For Hardy–Weinberg p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, carriers have frequency 0.48.
feature: For Hardy–Weinberg p = 0.60 and q = 0.40, carriers have frequency 0.48.
confusion: For this simple recessive model, carriers are heterozygotes, not all individuals with a.

meaning: A model-predicted number obtained by multiplying a frequency by population size.
example: A frequency of 0.48 in N = 200 gives 96 expected individuals.
importantDistinction: Expected counts need not be exactly realized in a finite sample.
whatItDoes: A frequency of 0.48 in N = 200 gives 96 expected individuals.
feature: A frequency of 0.48 in N = 200 gives 96 expected individuals.
confusion: Expected counts need not be exactly realized in a finite sample.

meaning: Recovering q from q² when the Hardy–Weinberg assumptions apply.
importantDistinction: Taking a square root is not the same as dividing the frequency by two.
confusion: Taking a square root is not the same as dividing the frequency by two.

meaning: A count actually supplied or measured in the sample.
example: A sample contains 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals.
importantDistinction: Observed and expected values must be kept separate.
whatItDoes: A sample contains 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals.
feature: A sample contains 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals.
confusion: Observed and expected values must be kept separate.

meaning: The genotype proportions predicted by the selected model.
example: For p = q = 0.50, Hardy–Weinberg predicts 0.25 AA, 0.50 Aa and 0.25 aa.
importantDistinction: A prediction can be compared with observations rather than substituted for them.
whatItDoes: For p = q = 0.50, Hardy–Weinberg predicts 0.25 AA, 0.50 Aa and 0.25 aa.
feature: For p = q = 0.50, Hardy–Weinberg predicts 0.25 AA, 0.50 Aa and 0.25 aa.
confusion: A prediction can be compared with observations rather than substituted for them.

meaning: Differences that arise because a finite sample does not reproduce population proportions perfectly.
example: Two small samples can show different counts by chance.
importantDistinction: A small mismatch is not automatically strong evidence of a specific mechanism.
whatItDoes: Two small samples can show different counts by chance.
feature: Two small samples can show different counts by chance.
confusion: A small mismatch is not automatically strong evidence of a specific mechanism.

meaning: Evaluation of how well observations fit a model’s predictions.
example: Observed heterozygotes are compared with the expected 2pq fraction.
importantDistinction: Agreement does not prove every assumption; mismatch does not identify one cause alone.
whatItDoes: Observed heterozygotes are compared with the expected 2pq fraction.
feature: Observed heterozygotes are compared with the expected 2pq fraction.
confusion: Agreement does not prove every assumption; mismatch does not identify one cause alone.

meaning: Differential reproductive success associated with heritable variation in a particular environment.
example: A heritable resistance trait improves survival and subsequent reproduction under a specific challenge.
importantDistinction: The environment influences which variants contribute more descendants.
whatItDoes: A heritable resistance trait improves survival and subsequent reproduction under a specific challenge.
feature: A heritable resistance trait improves survival and subsequent reproduction under a specific challenge.
confusion: The environment influences which variants contribute more descendants.

meaning: Reproductive contribution compared with other genotypes or phenotypes in the relevant setting.
example: One genotype leaves more surviving reproductive descendants under the stated conditions.
importantDistinction: Fitness is not simply physical strength or long life.
whatItDoes: One genotype leaves more surviving reproductive descendants under the stated conditions.
feature: One genotype leaves more surviving reproductive descendants under the stated conditions.
confusion: Fitness is not simply physical strength or long life.

meaning: Selection associated with differences in mating success.
example: A heritable courtship trait affects the probability of obtaining mates.
importantDistinction: A mating advantage can occur even when a trait has survival costs.
whatItDoes: A heritable courtship trait affects the probability of obtaining mates.
feature: A heritable courtship trait affects the probability of obtaining mates.
confusion: A mating advantage can occur even when a trait has survival costs.

meaning: Mating patterns that depend on characteristics related to the genotype being studied.
example: Individuals preferentially mate with others having a similar phenotype.
importantDistinction: It can alter genotype proportions without automatically changing allele frequencies by itself.
whatItDoes: Individuals preferentially mate with others having a similar phenotype.
feature: Individuals preferentially mate with others having a similar phenotype.
confusion: It can alter genotype proportions without automatically changing allele frequencies by itself.

meaning: Random change in allele frequencies caused by chance sampling in finite populations.
example: By chance, carriers of one allele leave fewer descendants in a small population.
importantDistinction: Drift does not require the allele to affect survival or mating success.
whatItDoes: By chance, carriers of one allele leave fewer descendants in a small population.
feature: By chance, carriers of one allele leave fewer descendants in a small population.
confusion: Drift does not require the allele to affect survival or mating success.

meaning: A change in genetic composition associated with a sharp reduction in population size.
example: A small surviving subset carries only part of the earlier variation.
importantDistinction: A demographic recovery does not automatically restore lost alleles.
whatItDoes: A small surviving subset carries only part of the earlier variation.
feature: A small surviving subset carries only part of the earlier variation.
confusion: A demographic recovery does not automatically restore lost alleles.

meaning: A change in allele representation when a small subset establishes a new population.
example: A few colonists carry frequencies different from the source population by chance.
importantDistinction: The original large population need not be destroyed.
whatItDoes: A few colonists carry frequencies different from the source population by chance.
feature: A few colonists carry frequencies different from the source population by chance.
confusion: The original large population need not be destroyed.

meaning: An allele reaching frequency 1 at the locus in the population considered.
example: Only A remains among sampled reproductive copies.
importantDistinction: Fixation describes the locus and population, not the absence of variation everywhere.
whatItDoes: Only A remains among sampled reproductive copies.
feature: Only A remains among sampled reproductive copies.
confusion: Fixation describes the locus and population, not the absence of variation everywhere.

meaning: Transfer of alleles between populations through successful genetic contribution.
example: Migrants reproduce in another population, introducing allele copies.
importantDistinction: Movement without reproduction does not necessarily change the next generation’s gene pool.
whatItDoes: Migrants reproduce in another population, introducing allele copies.
feature: Migrants reproduce in another population, introducing allele copies.
confusion: Movement without reproduction does not necessarily change the next generation’s gene pool.

meaning: The introduction of new sequence variants through mutation.
example: A heritable DNA change creates an allele not previously present at that locus.
importantDistinction: Mutation is a source of new alleles; selection acts on their consequences.
whatItDoes: A heritable DNA change creates an allele not previously present at that locus.
feature: A heritable DNA change creates an allele not previously present at that locus.
confusion: Mutation is a source of new alleles; selection acts on their consequences.

meaning: The degree to which populations exchange genetic contributions.
example: Reproductive movement connects two habitat patches.
importantDistinction: Physical connection is not the same as demonstrated successful gene flow.
whatItDoes: Reproductive movement connects two habitat patches.
feature: Reproductive movement connects two habitat patches.
confusion: Physical connection is not the same as demonstrated successful gene flow.

meaning: Differences in genetic composition among populations.
example: Two isolated populations have different allele frequencies.
importantDistinction: Gene flow can reduce differences, while isolation can allow them to increase.
whatItDoes: Two isolated populations have different allele frequencies.
feature: Two isolated populations have different allele frequencies.
confusion: Gene flow can reduce differences, while isolation can allow them to increase.

meaning: The variety of genetic variants represented in a population or set of populations.
example: A population contains several alleles at the loci examined.
importantDistinction: A larger head count does not guarantee recovery of previously lost variants.
whatItDoes: A population contains several alleles at the loci examined.
feature: A population contains several alleles at the loci examined.
confusion: A larger head count does not guarantee recovery of previously lost variants.

meaning: Mating between genetically related individuals.
example: Relatives are more likely to share copies inherited from a common ancestor.
importantDistinction: It can increase homozygosity without creating harmful alleles on demand.
whatItDoes: Relatives are more likely to share copies inherited from a common ancestor.
feature: Relatives are more likely to share copies inherited from a common ancestor.
confusion: It can increase homozygosity without creating harmful alleles on demand.

meaning: Observations used to evaluate a population’s condition and response to an action.
example: Breeding success, survival, connectivity and genetic markers are measured together.
importantDistinction: Several measures are needed to distinguish mechanisms and outcomes.
whatItDoes: Breeding success, survival, connectivity and genetic markers are measured together.
feature: Breeding success, survival, connectivity and genetic markers are measured together.
confusion: Several measures are needed to distinguish mechanisms and outcomes.

meaning: The capacity for heritable variation to support responses to changing conditions.
example: Standing variation can provide different responses to a new challenge.
importantDistinction: Genetic diversity can matter without guaranteeing survival under every change.
whatItDoes: Standing variation can provide different responses to a new challenge.
feature: Standing variation can provide different responses to a new challenge.
confusion: Genetic diversity can matter without guaranteeing survival under every change.
